title: A part can cross an old join
question: Does a part have to be one of the strokes you drew?
intro: Two strokes meet at 3. Move a length-two query across that join, then introduce a real gap.
try_it: Leave the query at 2.5: it crosses the old join at 3.
Switch on the gap. Move the query to 0 and compare.
notice: A drawing boundary and a gap have different effects. Joined collinear strokes fuse into one maximal line; missing line content makes some queries fail.
scope: Exact one-dimensional line shapes in the plane. The input strokes are shown only to explain their history; matching uses their geometric content.

sources.connection: The experiment makes maximal-line representation and coverage visible.

sources.locator: pp. 343–346: shapes, operations and labelled shapes
sources.connection: The part relation concerns embedded geometry, rather than original drawing objects.
A maximal-element representation does not exhaust the recognizable parts.

title: Add, erase, keep the overlap
question: What exactly is common to two line shapes?
intro: Keep A fixed. Move B, choose an operation, and compare the operands with the computed result.
try_it: Erase the middle of A to split it into two maximal lines.
Choose intersection, then turn B into a crossing line.
notice: Union keeps all line content. Difference removes common line content. Intersection retains shared intervals; a crossing point alone is not a one-dimensional line shape.
scope: This model contains line elements, without independent point elements. Difference uses the regularized line-shape convention: retained segments include their endpoints. These are geometric operations, not operations on a list of stroke IDs.

sources.connection: The worked controls illustrate the Boolean shape operations, without reproducing the paper’s data structures.
Compare shape sum and difference with ordinary set operations on stored elements.

title: One rule, one transformation
question: Why must both sides of a rule move together?
intro: The rule keeps a length-two line and adds a stem at its midpoint. Position its left side in the host; the same transformation positions the replacement.
try_it: Reflect across the horizontal axis: the match stays, but the stem flips.
Raise the query or turn it 90° and see why the rule cannot apply.
notice: First check t(A) ≤ S. Only then compute (S − t(A)) + t(B). A failed match has no rule result; placing the new stem independently would change the rule.
scope: A finite D₄ orientation menu, three rational scales and a half-unit translation grid. This is a project example, not a general continuous or parametric recognition algorithm.

sources.locator: pp. 347–349: grammar definition and square example
sources.connection: The matching and replacement stages use one shared transformation.
Registration and containment are distinct tasks in rule recognition.

sources.locator: Part 1: Anatomy of a Replacement Rule → Formal Definition
sources.connection: The tutorial states the same-transform replacement formula.
Q1 supplies the conceptual matching-and-replacement mechanism.

title: Same part, different consequences
question: Does one matched part imply one possible result?
intro: Compare the identity and a reflection. Both match the same line. Now change the rule from adding a stem to an identity rule.
try_it: Switch between the two matching transformations and watch the stem.
Use the identity rule and compare all three counts again.
notice: Distinct transformations may match the same geometric part. Their results can differ, or coincide. Counting transformations, parts and results answers three separate questions.
scope: Exactly eight orientations are tested, with scale 1 and translation (0,0). Counts are complete only for this declared menu, not for all possible continuous transformations.

sources.connection: The algebraic account separates shape geometry from the transformations under which rules apply.

sources.locator: Part 2: Scale, Angle and Single Line Case; parameter summary table
sources.connection: Matching depends on permitted transformations and additional choices.

title: Look again without moving a line
question: Can an identity rule matter if the drawing stays identical?
intro: Two adjacent squares also contain an outer rectangle. Choose a part and apply A → A; compare the highlighted reading with the unchanged drawing.
try_it: Choose the left square, then the right square.
Choose the outer rectangle and check the geometry comparison.
notice: The selected reading changes while the line geometry remains equal. This makes the difference between recognizing a part and altering a shape explicit.
scope: Three supplied readings of a fixed drawing. These are not all its parts, and the interface does not measure perception or claim a psychological effect.

sources.connection: The schema A → A makes a part recognition explicit without moving geometry.
The retrospective distinguishes identity-based analysis from addition-based generation.
Q2 discusses identities for symmetry and parsing.
The abstract motivates the identity-rule question. This original diagram does not reconstruct the unread note.
A related question is which newly recognized shapes can become inputs. The abstract’s special-rule system is not implemented here.

title: Same square, different possibilities
question: What changes when you change the available rules?
intro: Start with one square. A right rule or an up rule adds a neighboring square beside the currently marked one. Build a short trace, then try a different rule menu.
try_it: Build a staircase by alternating right and up.
Choose right only. The trace resets; try to make the same staircase.
notice: Choices within one rule menu produce different traces. Changing the menu changes what can be generated. A fixed square vocabulary alone does not determine a design language.
scope: An original planar toy grammar, with a visible focus marker and an eight-step exploration cap. Rules use exact line arithmetic. Only the marked square is selected; this does not search all possible embeddings or reproduce Froebel’s solids or a historical building grammar.

sources.connection: The first exercise derives languages from a vocabulary and spatial relations.
The constructive programme separates vocabulary, spatial relations, rules and initial shapes.
The survey explains why authoring and revising rules can make design choices explicit.

sources.locator: pp. 13–18: Alberti, shape grammars and four strategies; Fig. 4
sources.connection: Compare varying designs under rules with changing the rules themselves. This toy demonstrates the distinction, not the paper’s architectural cases.

title: Thickness has rules too
question: When weighted lines overlap, should their weights add?
intro: Change two numerical weights on overlapping intervals. Compare maximum-based sum, minimum-based intersection and clipped difference.
try_it: Give both lines weight 3: their sum still has weight 3 in the overlap.
Set A to 2 and B to 4, then subtract B from A.
notice: In this numerical model, sum uses max(a,b), intersection uses min(a,b), and difference uses max(a−b,0) where both lines occur. Zero weight removes that interval from the result.
scope: Positive integer weights on collinear intervals. Stroke widths visualize the chosen formal values; they are not physical mass, optical ink mixing or a general model of material behavior.

sources.connection: The numerical operations and subdivision of overlaps are the source concept.

title: Who wins in the overlap?
question: Does geometry alone decide what an overlap means?
intro: Two fields use different hatch patterns. Change their priority and inspect only the shared region.
try_it: Give field A higher priority, then give it to B.
Compare the fixed outlines and the changing overlap pattern.
notice: The regions stay in place. Their ranking changes the quality assigned to their intersection. A visible boundary alone cannot supply that decision.
scope: A two-field priority toy inspired by the need for an explicit overlap convention. It does not reproduce Knight’s full color-field algebra, her layering/weaving figures, material physics or additive color mixing. Hatching is used to keep the site monochrome.

sources.locator: Color grammars: an informal discussion; rankings and Figures 12–16
sources.connection: Knight supplies explicit ranking conventions for coincident qualities; the controls isolate that general issue.

sources.locator: History: Original Design—Color Grammars; final paragraphs
sources.connection: The color-grammar discussion connects spatial rules to qualitative information.

title: Build sets and compare them
question: Which elements survive each set operation?
intro: Tap elements to put them in A or B. Change the operation and watch the result, including ordered pairs and the power set.
try_it: Remove every element from A and inspect its power set.
Compare A × B with A ∩ B: ordered pairs are different objects from their components.
notice: Set membership ignores ordering and duplicates. A × B contains ordered pairs; P(A) contains subsets. The empty set has one subset: itself.
scope: A fixed four-element universe. This is finite set arithmetic, not an illustration of paradoxes or a proof about arbitrary infinite sets.

sources.connection: The selected set chapters distinguish elements, subsets and power sets.
Small finite sets make the definitions and counting behavior visible.

sources.locator: Introduction and §1.1, printed pp.3–6; Chapter 4 pp.81–89
sources.connection: The selected sets/functions chapter provides the foundational definitions.

title: Choose what counts as the same
question: How does a relation turn elements into classes?
intro: Group 0 through 5 by their remainder after division. Change the modulus and compare two selected elements.
try_it: With modulus 3, compare 2 and 5.
Switch to modulus 4 and inspect the different class sizes.
notice: Two numbers are related exactly when they have the same remainder. Every number belongs to one class; different classes are disjoint.
scope: Congruence restricted to the finite set {0,1,2,3,4,5}. These are equivalence classes of that set, not a construction of quotient-group multiplication. Classes need not have equal sizes here.

sources.connection: The selected relation section introduces equivalence and classes.
Equivalence is defined through reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity.
The equivalence discussion motivates partitions; later quotient operations require additional checks.

title: One arrow from every input
question: When is a function a reversible pairing?
intro: Choose one output for each of a, b and c. Inspect collisions and unused outputs.
try_it: Use the cycle preset: each output has exactly one incoming arrow.
Use the collision preset and find both the repeated output and the unused one.
notice: Injective means no collisions. Surjective means every declared output is reached. A bijection has both properties, so each output identifies one input.
scope: Functions from the three-element set {a,b,c} to itself. For these equal finite sizes, injectivity and surjectivity coincide; they need not coincide for arbitrary domain/codomain choices. A bijection here is a permutation.

sources.connection: The functions section separates domain, codomain, injection and surjection.
The map definitions explain collisions and coverage of the codomain.

sources.locator: Introduction and §1.1, printed pp.3–6; Chapter 4 pp.81–89
sources.connection: The selected definitions treat functions as assignments with stated domains and codomains.

title: Try the other order
question: Does reflecting then turning equal turning then reflecting?
intro: Track the same four labelled corners through B, then A. Compare that with reversing the order.
try_it: Use quarter turn and reflection; compare the final labels.
Set A to the identity and compare again.
notice: AB means apply B first, then A. The unlabelled square looks the same after every symmetry; the corner labels reveal where its points went.
scope: D₄ is the eight-element symmetry group of a square. These are rigid motions with no scaling. This does not model every spatial transformation or a crystallographic classification.

sources.connection: Rigid symmetries and composition motivate the group laws and noncommutativity.
The first lecture motivates groups through composing symmetries.

title: What moves, what stays fixed?
question: Why do eight symmetries not always give eight different point positions?
intro: Choose a point and a square symmetry. Compare all its possible images with the operations that leave that point fixed.
try_it: Compare a corner with the center.
Choose the general point (2,1) and check 8 = orbit size × stabilizer size.
notice: The orbit counts distinct positions. The stabilizer counts transformations fixing the chosen point. For this finite action, their sizes multiply to the group order 8.
scope: The standard action of D₄ on points in the plane. The general point lies outside the square; the square supplies the symmetry operations. This is a small action example, not a simulation of the Monster or a proof of the general theorem.

sources.connection: The selected group-action section introduces orbits.
Chapter 4 defines actions and stabilizers.
Lecture 23 supplies the action, orbit and stabilizer framework.

title: Can your selection be a group?
question: Can any collection of square symmetries form a group?
intro: Toggle transformations into a selection. Check whether composition and inversion stay inside it.
try_it: Start with identity and a quarter turn. Find the missing product.
Try all rotations, then build a two-element reflection subgroup.
notice: A subgroup uses the same operation as D₄. It needs the identity, closure and inverses. Associativity is inherited from D₄; it is not an extra property supplied by the selection.
scope: All subsets of the eight known D₄ transformations are small enough to check directly. This is a test inside a known group, not a method for certifying an arbitrary operation table.

sources.connection: The group axioms and dihedral examples motivate checking identity, composition and inverses.
The opening group framework supplies the operation and axioms.
